newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Tax cut insufficiant to boost Yugo car sales.
newsitem.headline: Tax cut insufficiant to boost Yugo car sales.

text.p: Yugoslav car dealers, facing a daunting task to sell in a slumping market, said on Tuesday a recent import tax cut was not enough to dispel their gloomy prospects.

"It (the tax reduction) will not have any significant impact on car sales. It will not increase the number of potential buyers nor will it influence them to choose better cars," said one industry source who asked not to be named.
"Funds here are scarce and exhausted. People simply do not have the money to invest in expensive cars," said the source.
The Yugoslav government as of Monday reduced import duties on new passenger cars with engines between 1500-3000 cc to 53.75 percent from the previous 77 percent.
The measure will be valid only until the adoption of a new law on customs tariffs announced for the beginning of July.
Analysts agreed that the government, struggling to return to the international market after four years of U.N. trade embargo, was under pressure from abroad to open its market.
"The measure is aimed both to protect country's car maker Zastava and satisfy needs of buyers of cars and commercial vehicles that are not produced locally," the source said.
But the country's car maker Zastava, sharing the destiny of the entire economy on the verge of collapse, last year made only five percent of its pre-sanction 200,000 cars output.
Out of a targetted output of 22,250 cars this year, 10,000 were earmarked for sale at home.
Zastava saw the measure as just another threat to its existence and sales despite the fact that it produces only small Yugo cars.
"This just fuels car importers' expectations on a further liberalisation of the market," said Zastava Group vice-president Slobodan Radovic.
But he insisted that second-hand car imports from Croatia and Bosnia with one percent customs duties were a bigger threat.
"That is a serious threat to the entire car sales in the country. And that must be stopped." Radovic said.

Some 150,000 second-hand cars are believed to have entered the country since last autumn. Despite age and mileage, they are cheaper and therefore attractive to the domestic buyer whose average monthly wage slumped to 200-250 German marks.
Yugoslavia's Renault dealer Renault Kep said its sales were crippled by second-hand car imports and were down to 30 percent over the same period last year.

General manager of Renault Kep Velimir Pijevic saw high prices of imported cars, lack of credits and low purchasing power as the main reasons for such "catastrophic" sales and doubted anything could improve this year.
A growing crime rate was also hampering sales.
"It is difficult to find customers willing to risk having an attractive car with so much theft around," said one trader.

But luxury car dealers were not in the same boat and Autocommerce selling Volkswagen and Audi models with prices ranging from 12,000-150,000 German marks (pre-tax) said their sales was booming with more than 100 percent rise over 1996.
"Each car has its buyer. This market is simply hungry for our models and it has an enormous potential," said company's sales manager Ljiljana Gacesa, but gave no more details.
"There are quite a lot of status-conscious businessmen willing to pay huge ammounts of money to own good quality vehicles. Interest for the latest Audi 6 is enormous," she added.

Car imports stood at some $42 million in 1996. Importers say there is a great need for high quality cars in a market where the average age of about 1.2 million cars in the country is 10 years and some 40 percent are older than 12 years.
Traders agreed 1997 import quota of some 6,000 cars for all the importers would not be used mainly due to the poor economy.
"Even if we manage to sell something, then we have problems to collect the money," said one trader.
-- Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom +381 11 222 4254
